chapters.summary: Council Member Encarnación says she has worked on the project for years and praises its 100% affordability, senior housing, waterfront access, park space, dog run, and Passive House design. She expresses support and looks forward to questioning the development team.
chapters.title: Council Member Encarnación supports 100% affordable Bronx waterfront project

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Good afternoon, and thank you, Chair, for the opportunity to give a statement regarding this proposal.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: I have been involved with this project for many years.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: In fact, when I first joined the office of the previous Deputy Speaker, this project was part of my portfolio.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Having not only followed its progress, but actively engaged in it, I've had the opportunity to witness the commitment and collaboration that have gone into bringing this development forward.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Throughout this process, the project team, the development partners, HPD, they have all worked alongside our office and the community to ensure that this project is responsive to the needs of the neighborhood.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: This included establishing a community advisory board, conducting multiple site visits, and working to ensure that important neighborhood concerns, including traffic and transportation considerations, were brought to the attention of the Department of Transportation.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: In the Bronx, many waterfront developments have been developed, and unfortunately, many of them did not take advantage of the HPD subsidies that would have brought in more affordable housing to the district.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: This project, however, is 100% affordable, has dedicated senior housing, permits greater access to our waterfront, provides public park space, as well as a dog run, and as a proud member of the Animal Caucus, I support.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: for that, as well as environmentally sustainable development through its passive house design, which for the South Bronx is particularly important.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: This is exactly the kind of investments that our community in the Bronx needs and deserves.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: We need development that does more than simply add housing.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: We need projects that thoughtfully addresses the needs of existing residents, creates opportunities, improves our neighborhoods, and contributes to a more sustainable future.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: I'm happy that we are finally at this point of the process, and I'm confident that the answers to the questions asked today will prove that this development will be a great benefit to this district.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: So I'm here to ask questions.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: I am in support of this project, and I'm looking forward to the conversation.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Justin Dolan of HPD presents the site south of the Madison Avenue Bridge between the Major Deegan and the Harlem River. He notes three tax lots: one privately owned former auto auction building and two city-owned lots leased to a moving company.
chapters.title: HPD presents site location and existing conditions for 63 Exterior Street

utterances.speaker: Justin Dolan
utterances.text: Good morning, Chair Marte and members of the subcommittee.

utterances.speaker: Justin Dolan
utterances.text: We're very pleased to be here to present this project for you today.

utterances.speaker: Justin Dolan
utterances.text: My name is Justin Donlan.

utterances.speaker: Justin Dolan
utterances.text: I'm the Deputy Director of Land Use and Stakeholder Engagement for the Government Affairs Division at HPD.

utterances.speaker: Justin Dolan
utterances.text: Filling in for fan favorite Ted Weinstein.

utterances.speaker: Justin Dolan
utterances.text: So if you go to the first slide, please.

utterances.speaker: Justin Dolan
utterances.text: So as you can see here, the development site is located just south of the Madison Avenue Bridge between the Major Deegan Expressway and the river.

utterances.speaker: Justin Dolan
utterances.text: And if you could head over to the next slide, please.

utterances.speaker: Justin Dolan
utterances.text: So the site's comprised of three tax lots.

utterances.speaker: Justin Dolan
utterances.text: One is privately owned by the development team, and two lots are city-owned.

utterances.speaker: Justin Dolan
utterances.text: Today, the privately owned lot contains a vacant former auto auction building, which you can see in the frame there as is labeled, which will ultimately be demolished to make way for the new housing.

utterances.speaker: Justin Dolan
utterances.text: The two city-owned lots are currently occupied by the padded wagon moving company, which the city leases.

utterances.speaker: Justin Dolan
utterances.text: And if you could proceed to the next slide.

chapters.summary: Dolan explains that recent waterfront rezonings produced little affordable housing because developments did not use HPD programs. He lists required UDAAP, disposition, and waterfront-related actions for the project.
chapters.title: HPD outlines rezoning context and required land use actions

utterances.speaker: Justin Dolan
utterances.text: So since the city's rezonings, the waterfront and lower concourse have experienced a wave of new development, which is illustrated on the map here.

utterances.speaker: Justin Dolan
utterances.text: These developments, however, did not utilize HPD programs, and as a result, they have produced relatively little affordable housing.

utterances.speaker: Justin Dolan
utterances.text: So what that means is we have a real opportunity here to provide a transformative project and an opportunity to reshape that dynamic by introducing a significant number of 100% affordable housing units on the waterfront.

utterances.speaker: Justin Dolan
utterances.text: If you could proceed to the next slide.

utterances.speaker: Justin Dolan
utterances.text: So there's a number of UERP and related actions required to facilitate development of this project.

utterances.speaker: Justin Dolan
utterances.text: And that includes UERP land use actions, including the disposition of city-owned land and an urban development action area designation.

utterances.speaker: Justin Dolan
utterances.text: And additionally, because of the unique shape of the waterfront, the site calls for additional actions to ensure that the proposed development meets applicable waterfront requirements.

utterances.speaker: Justin Dolan
utterances.text: We can go to the next slide.

chapters.summary: Rhea Tong of Douglaston Development introduces the joint venture with Phipps Houses. She describes 183 senior units in the north building and about 350 family units in the south building, with rents up to 80% AMI and average incomes below 50% AMI.
chapters.title: Douglaston and Phipps present 537-unit affordable housing program

utterances.speaker: Rhea Tong
utterances.text: Thank you, Justin.

utterances.speaker: Rhea Tong
utterances.text: Hi, I'm Rhea Tong with Douglaston Development.

utterances.speaker: Rhea Tong
utterances.text: Our development team is a joint venture between FIPS Houses and Douglaston Development.

utterances.speaker: Rhea Tong
utterances.text: FIPS is a nonprofit affordable housing developer with an affiliate social services company, FIPS Neighborhoods, and Douglaston Development is a New York City-based development company with affiliate construction and management companies.

utterances.speaker: Rhea Tong
utterances.text: Next slide, please.

utterances.speaker: Rhea Tong
utterances.text: The development will bring over 500 new affordable housing units to this waterfront site.

utterances.speaker: Rhea Tong
utterances.text: The north building will consist of 183 units of affordable senior housing, and the south building will consist of approximately 350 units of affordable housing geared predominantly for families.

utterances.speaker: Rhea Tong
utterances.text: We anticipate the development will be financed through HPD and HDC's affordable housing programs.

utterances.speaker: Rhea Tong
utterances.text: We also anticipate the capital stack to include investment tax credits for geothermal and solar arrays and brownfield tax credits.

utterances.speaker: Rhea Tong
utterances.text: Rents will be set at a maximum of 80% of AMI with incomes ranging, averaging below 50% of AMI.

utterances.speaker: Rhea Tong
utterances.text: There will be retail space programmed at the North Building, community facility space programmed at the South Building, and dedicated on-site social service space at the North Building as well.

utterances.speaker: Rhea Tong
utterances.text: Next slide, please.

chapters.summary: Tong highlights the shared lobby with 24/7 security and its goal of intergenerational community. She also describes over 25,000 square feet of shore public walkway, 8,000 square feet of additional open space, and a shared street on East 138th Street.
chapters.title: Development team details shared lobby and waterfront open space

utterances.speaker: Rhea Tong
utterances.text: A big feature of this development is the shared lobby.

utterances.speaker: Rhea Tong
utterances.text: It's designed to be transparent to encourage visibility of the waterfront for pedestrians and visibility of the street from within the lobby.

utterances.speaker: Rhea Tong
utterances.text: The shared lobby will also have 24-7 front desk security presence.

utterances.speaker: Rhea Tong
utterances.text: The philosophy of this shared lobby is twofold.

utterances.speaker: Rhea Tong
utterances.text: First, it's to improve safety and security at the site, and secondly, it's to promote intergenerational connections and foster a sense of community by having the senior building residents and the family building residents enter from a common entrance.

utterances.speaker: Rhea Tong
utterances.text: Next slide, please.

utterances.speaker: Rhea Tong
utterances.text: Another big feature of this project is the public open space we are bringing to the waterfront.

utterances.speaker: Rhea Tong
utterances.text: We'll be introducing over 25,000 square feet of shore public walkway space.

utterances.speaker: Rhea Tong
utterances.text: We'll also be providing an additional 8,000 square feet of public open space.

utterances.speaker: Rhea Tong
utterances.text: In addition, we're designing a shared street along East 138th Street that will predominantly serve pedestrians and incorporate various landscaping and beautification.

utterances.speaker: Rhea Tong
utterances.text: Next slide, please.

chapters.summary: Tong walks through renderings of the site's south end, including the dog run, play area, and fitness areas. She notes the site's adjacency to the Oak Point Link freight rail line and shows the waterfront view from the Harlem River.
chapters.title: Rendering walkthrough highlights Oak Point Link and active waterfront uses

utterances.speaker: Rhea Tong
utterances.text: This is a view south and shows the access to the waterfront from the north end of the site.

utterances.speaker: Rhea Tong
utterances.text: It also illustrates the adjacency to the Oak Point Link.

utterances.speaker: Rhea Tong
utterances.text: The Oak Point Link is a freight rail line with trains that run approximately once or twice a day.

utterances.speaker: Rhea Tong
utterances.text: Next slide, please.

utterances.speaker: Rhea Tong
utterances.text: And this is a visual of the southern end of the site where much of the active programming is sited.

utterances.speaker: Rhea Tong
utterances.text: You can see the dog run located in the foreground of the site and the play area and fitness areas behind that.

utterances.speaker: Rhea Tong
utterances.text: Next slide, please.

utterances.speaker: Rhea Tong
utterances.text: And here's a view of the waterfront from the Harlem River.

utterances.speaker: Rhea Tong
utterances.text: And next I'll pass it along to Nina.

chapters.summary: Nina Villanueva of Phipps Houses presents the project's sustainable and resilient design. Both buildings will meet Passive House standards, use solar and geothermal energy, and be raised over four feet above the required base flood elevation.
chapters.title: Phipps presents Passive House and flood-resilience features

utterances.speaker: Nina Villanueva
utterances.text: Hello, my name is Nina Villanueva.

utterances.speaker: Nina Villanueva
utterances.text: I'm with Phipps Houses, and I will continue our presentation, starting by discussing the project's sustainable and resilient design.

utterances.speaker: Nina Villanueva
utterances.text: Both buildings will be designed to Passive House standards and will also be using renewable energy in the form of solar panels and geothermal heat pumps.

utterances.speaker: Nina Villanueva
utterances.text: The project also has a number of green infrastructure elements, including hundreds of feet of new plantings along East 135th Street, the shared street, and the short public walkway.

utterances.speaker: Nina Villanueva
utterances.text: Additionally, given the project's close proximity to the water, our design also implements flood and stormwater mitigation components, including raising the buildings above the 100-year floodplain.

utterances.speaker: Nina Villanueva
utterances.text: The base flood elevation requirement is 11 feet, and our development is 15.4 feet, making it over 4 feet higher than required.

utterances.speaker: Nina Villanueva
utterances.text: The project has water to the west of it and a pretty busy intersection to the east, which is why we'll also be implementing a number of site circulation improvements, which I will talk about on the next slide.

utterances.speaker: Nina Villanueva
utterances.text: Next slide.

chapters.summary: Villanueva details site circulation improvements, including widened sidewalks, a planted buffer between pedestrians and bikes, bollards, and a loading zone. She also introduces a proposed senior shuttle with a route designed around health clinics, grocery stores, and banks.
chapters.title: Phipps details pedestrian, bike, loading, and senior shuttle circulation

utterances.speaker: Nina Villanueva
utterances.text: Next slide, please.

utterances.speaker: Nina Villanueva
utterances.text: So from this chart, you can see the waste pickup area in blue.

utterances.speaker: Nina Villanueva
utterances.text: We'll also be widening the sidewalks to facilitate a protected pedestrian area, which wraps around the entire development in red.

utterances.speaker: Nina Villanueva
utterances.text: And then on East 135th Street, the pedestrian area will be bifurcated from the purple bike area by a planted buffer zone.

utterances.speaker: Nina Villanueva
utterances.text: And then we'll also have bollards at medians and corners of the sidewalk.

utterances.speaker: Nina Villanueva
utterances.text: In yellow, we have our loading zone, and that's designed for convenience and safety and will also be used as a bike dismount area.

utterances.speaker: Nina Villanueva
utterances.text: Additionally, the space will also be used as a pickup and drop-off location for our proposed senior shuttle.

utterances.speaker: Nina Villanueva
utterances.text: Next slide, please.

utterances.speaker: Nina Villanueva
utterances.text: This is our proposed shuttle route, and it was designed with input from local members of the community to include health clinics, grocery stores, and retail banks.

utterances.speaker: Nina Villanueva
utterances.text: It also includes stops at local senior facilities to promote integration within the surrounding community.

chapters.summary: Villanueva explains changes to the family building's unit mix, adding one- and two-bedroom units and nearly doubling HPD's minimum for family-sized units. She also presents AMI rents and summarizes five years of community engagement.
chapters.title: Phipps outlines unit mix changes, AMI rents, and community engagement

utterances.speaker: Nina Villanueva
utterances.text: Next slide, please.

utterances.speaker: Nina Villanueva
utterances.text: Moving over to our unit mix, we have building one, which is intended to be our senior building.

utterances.speaker: Nina Villanueva
utterances.text: So we have a mix of studios and one bedrooms.

utterances.speaker: Nina Villanueva
utterances.text: Building two is intended for families.

utterances.speaker: Nina Villanueva
utterances.text: And so we have a mix of studios, ones, twos, and threes.

utterances.speaker: Nina Villanueva
utterances.text: Based on council member and community feedback, we've made changes to the unit mix in the family building, which also contributes to an overall balance between both buildings.

utterances.speaker: Nina Villanueva
utterances.text: Decreased the amount of studios and added eight one bedrooms and 11 two bedrooms, nearly doubling HPD's term sheet minimum for twos and three bedrooms.

utterances.speaker: Nina Villanueva
utterances.text: As a result, we have lost a handful of units, but we did want to incorporate feedback from the community and accommodate more family-sized units.

utterances.speaker: Nina Villanueva
utterances.text: And one last note on this slide is each building will have its own on-site super.

utterances.speaker: Nina Villanueva
utterances.text: Next slide, please.

utterances.speaker: Nina Villanueva
utterances.text: So moving on to the 2026 AMIs, this chart shows the yearly income and monthly rents for the AMI tiers we are incorporating in the building.

utterances.speaker: Nina Villanueva
utterances.text: From this chart, you can see that a person renting a one-bedroom earning 50% of AMI will pay $1,369 a month in rent.

utterances.speaker: Nina Villanueva
utterances.text: Next slide, please.

utterances.speaker: Nina Villanueva
utterances.text: And lastly, we'd like to close with a summary of community engagement we've done to date, spanning back the past five years.

utterances.speaker: Nina Villanueva
utterances.text: We've spoken to council members, senior centers, and community boards, and we've actually updated this slide since our CPC presentation to include further engagement that we've done this past year.

utterances.speaker: Nina Villanueva
utterances.text: We think this project is responsive to the needs of our community, and we look forward to what's to come with this development.

utterances.speaker: Nina Villanueva
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.title: Marte asks how family-sized units were added in Building 2

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: Thank you for the presentation.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: I just want to add we've been joined by Council Member Aviles and Council Member Thomas Henry as well.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: I have a few questions before I kick it to the local council member.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: The unit mix in Building 2 has been updated to increase the number of family size units.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: Can you please explain how your team was able to make this happen?

utterances.speaker: Rhea Tong
utterances.text: We reorganized the layouts within the South building and combined.

utterances.speaker: Rhea Tong
utterances.text: Our architect can speak in more detail, but we reorganized the layouts to adjust to include more two- and three-bedroom units.

utterances.speaker: Rhea Tong
utterances.text: So using existing studios in one bedrooms and combining spaces to include more two and threes.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Sorry, if you're going to...

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Can you state your name for the record, please?

utterances.speaker: John Woelfling
utterances.text: John Wolfing.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: And can you please raise your right hand, sorry.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: And can you affirm to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth in your testimony before the subcommittee and an answer to all council member questions?

utterances.speaker: John Woelfling
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: John Woelfling
utterances.text: So I really don't have much to add to that.

utterances.speaker: John Woelfling
utterances.text: Ray covered it very well.

utterances.speaker: John Woelfling
utterances.text: But it was essentially, you know, the volume of the building, the south building, is fixed.

utterances.speaker: John Woelfling
utterances.text: The bulk of it is fixed.

utterances.speaker: John Woelfling
utterances.text: So we had to shuffle things around within the building, combine units, lose a few units, as it was indicated in the presentation.

utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

chapters.summary: Marte asks why the senior building includes many studios and whether they differ from traditional shoebox studios. Woelfling says units meet HPD design standards with ample daylight and large windows, while Tong notes the need to maximize senior households served.
chapters.title: Marte questions senior building studio design and HPD standards

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: In contrast, the senior housing building still includes a number, includes a substantial number of studio apartments.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: What drove the decision to include so many studios for seniors?

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: Are there design elements, layouts, or amendments?

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: that make these units different from the small traditional shoebox studios that we think of when we typically hear the word studio.

utterances.speaker: John Woelfling
utterances.text: I'll take some of that, and then I can take some of it as well.

utterances.speaker: Rhea Tong
utterances.text: Yeah, maybe.

utterances.speaker: John Woelfling
utterances.text: I'll start.

utterances.speaker: John Woelfling
utterances.text: So the units are designed to comply with HPD's design standards, and it's a very difficult balance.

utterances.speaker: John Woelfling
utterances.text: You don't want to go too big because that means you're being wasteful with the limited square footage that you have.

utterances.speaker: John Woelfling
utterances.text: So we do try to make these units as efficient as possible with ample daylight, large windows.

utterances.speaker: John Woelfling
utterances.text: You can see that from the renderings.

utterances.speaker: John Woelfling
utterances.text: So the quality of the daylight that comes into these spaces is really important for making a wonderful place to live.

utterances.speaker: John Woelfling
utterances.text: But we do have some units that balance those demands of having the maximum number of units that you can have, but also meeting HPD's design requirements.

utterances.speaker: Rhea Tong
utterances.text: And to add to that, in terms of the households for the North Building, we are also prioritizing maximizing the households we can serve.

utterances.speaker: Rhea Tong

chapters.summary: Al Gates supports expanding affordable housing but raises concerns about misleading market-rate language, permanent affordability, Phipps Houses management record, environmental testing, and oversight. He asks the Council to investigate and to establish a community and tenant oversight committee.
chapters.title: Al Gates raises affordability, management, and environmental concerns

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Al Gates
utterances.text: I support the initiative of expanding affordable housing, but I have some questions and concerns related to the project.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Al Gates
utterances.text: First, while reviewing the joint waterfront permit application, I noticed several times it describes the proposed project as providing both low-income and market-rate housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Al Gates
utterances.text: The likely explanation of what is intended by this is to say that the waterfront will serve the market-raised house residents.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Al Gates
utterances.text: However, the use of the word provide is misleading, and I would appreciate it if the subcommittee could investigate why this language appears and clarify its intended meaning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Al Gates
utterances.text: Additionally, given a for-profit company is proposing the transfer of publicly owned land, I second Bronx's borough president's request that before the council signs off on anything, they secure a legally binding agreement that guarantees each apartment permanently stays affordable,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Al Gates
utterances.text: even if property changes ownership.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Al Gates
utterances.text: Next, I'd like to raise some concerns regarding Phipps Houses Management under Lambert Houses.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Al Gates
utterances.text: Not only has it had to make settlements following a federal class action lawsuit from tenants,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Al Gates
utterances.text: But following 20 different tenant allegations in 2024, Bronx Community Board 6 has asked the council to, quote, seriously consider whether FIPS houses has the capacity to provide

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Al Gates
utterances.text: management services, end quote, and express concerns that, quote, more units for FIPS to take care of will mean the potential for further mismanagement, end quote.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Al Gates
utterances.text: It was then given an unsatisfactory management score of 59 out of 100, and federal audit was unanimously requested.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Al Gates
utterances.text: This audit exists in no databases, and while I've requested the documentation, I think investigation into if that audit was ever conducted and what its findings were would be appropriate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Al Gates
utterances.text: I've reviewed independent audits that identified a few reoccurring violations that I believe warrant further investigation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Al Gates
utterances.text: For example, the 2024 audit found Lambert Houses used more than $83,000 of its own funds to cover expenses for 28 Boston Roads Associate without HDUD approval.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Al Gates
utterances.text: This is one of the companies involved in cleaning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Al Gates
utterances.text: up contaminated land on Lambert Houses' previous properties.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Al Gates
utterances.text: Furthermore, all the other companies are FIPS associated, possibly creating conflict of interest.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Al Gates
utterances.text: I haven't been able to find the records of the environmental testing that should have been published for this land.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Al Gates
utterances.text: Given that Madison Landing also involves contaminated land, I think it would be appropriate that it be looked into before moving on with development.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Al Gates
utterances.text: I'd also like to confirm that the Madison Landings environmental remediation plans will be reviewed and approved by the Department of Health and the Department of Environmental Conservation before the council approves the development.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Al Gates
utterances.text: Lastly, given the risks associated with this project, I would like to advocate for the council to ask the HPD to establish a committee with community and tenant representation to oversee the project.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Al Gates
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: Thank you for your remarks.

utterances.text: Since I took office in 2022, School District 30 has faced overcrowding, long overdue new schools, and a rapidly growing community of young families.

utterances.text: The Baccalaureate School of Global Education is so crowded that they use the cafeteria for their learning space, for elective classes, and for gym, as well as their lunchroom.

utterances.text: And I do want to clarify, because I think I misspoke earlier, both buildings are 2031.

utterances.speaker: Kelly Murphy
utterances.text: I think I might have said 2030 on the other one.

utterances.speaker: Kelly Murphy

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Okay, so it's going to be 2031 for both BSGE and for Lehman.

utterances.speaker: Kelly Murphy
utterances.text: 11Th Street, yes.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Yeah, I could see why parents are going to be upset because it's a long, far, far away.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: And for school capacity in District 30, 1LIC created a need for 1,300 new elementary school seats in LIC, and the city has committed to building two new schools, two new elementary schools to meet this need.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: How does SCA plan to address this remaining elementary school seat need if the 11th site district, I mean, 11 sites...

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: The Schumann site on 11th Street is no longer being developed as an elementary school, so we're still short the number of school seats that we were promised.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: And the other site in Queensbridge South also has fallen apart.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: So what additional sites has SCA identified within the district for future elementary school capacity, such as the DOT site that was also given as was cited as or was referred to as an option because it wasn't cited.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: for elementary school capacity and what is the status of the DOT site on Annabelle Basin?

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: That was a potential elementary school site.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: And what is going to happen to make up for the lack of now almost half of those 1,300 school seats that were promised?

utterances.speaker: Kelly Murphy

utterances.text: So yes, the Long Island City is going to generate over 14,000 new housing units, which in turn generate new school seats.

utterances.speaker: Kelly Murphy
utterances.text: The build year for that is 2035.

utterances.speaker: Kelly Murphy
utterances.text: So as the housing comes online, then the school seat will come online.

utterances.speaker: Kelly Murphy
utterances.text: So that housing hasn't been developed yet.

utterances.speaker: Kelly Murphy
utterances.text: It will, over the next decade, will come online.

utterances.speaker: Kelly Murphy
utterances.text: In terms of finding additional sites, as I mentioned before, we work with brokers.

utterances.speaker: Kelly Murphy
utterances.text: We're lucky folks send us options.

utterances.speaker: Kelly Murphy
utterances.text: We're out, my staff's out looking, driving around, looking for undeveloped sites, if we could do assemblages.

utterances.speaker: Kelly Murphy
utterances.text: We're kind of revisiting old sites that maybe didn't work so great, but maybe

chapters.summary: Won asks how SCA informed the community and PTAs about the change to a middle school. Murphy describes standard site selection notices and hearings; Familian says SCA presented at CEC meetings, but Won notes the PTAs and Hunters Point Middle School were not notified.
chapters.title: Won questions outreach to PTAs about middle school change

utterances.speaker: Roberto Perez
utterances.text: Maybe we can think, be more creative and look at some old sites that we looked at in the past.

utterances.speaker: Roberto Perez
utterances.text: In terms of the DOT site, I know you've had some correspondence with our president.

utterances.speaker: Roberto Perez
utterances.text: That is a site used by DOT still currently, and they have their operations.

utterances.speaker: Roberto Perez
utterances.text: They have started the process, I understand, to start looking for an alternative site.

utterances.speaker: Roberto Perez
utterances.text: They've yet to secure the funding, so I think the time frame is open due to that.

utterances.speaker: Roberto Perez
utterances.text: But we're committed to working with DOT and our partners at New York City Public Schools to continue to engage that process and try to advocate to move that along.

utterances.speaker: Roberto Perez

utterances.speaker: Roberto Perez

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: We're already behind thousands of school seats in Long Island City because for decades we were told.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: That it was going to take 10 years for the apartments to be built.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: That was not true.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: The apartments are built within three years, on average, in Long Island City.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: We've built more apartments than the city of Los Angeles has done in the last decade.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: So for you to tell my parents that we're not going to build schools because we don't expect the apartments to be fully built by 2035 is a lie.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: And it's also a slap in our face because I know for a fact, even the schools that we're citing today are not going to be open until 2031.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: That is now another five years for my kids to have no school seats, as in like even my own kids.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: So if we're...

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: We're expecting 14,000 new units of housing.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: We're not going to wait until 2035.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won

utterances.text: And that's going to be at 4459 45th Avenue, which we have multiple recordings of the city of New York telling us that the DOT public site would be both housing for affordable housing, 100% affordable housing, as well as a new school.

chapters.summary: Won says parents are unhappy and asks for the Schumann timeline. Murphy gives a similar schedule to the other site, with closing in January, authorization in February, design, bidding, and construction; she corrects that both schools are expected in 2031, not 2030.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: The CECs are watching.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: And we're going to continue to fight until this administration gives us every single school seat that is owed to my district because we have taken on the brunt of building new housing for the entire city of New York, but we have not been given infrastructure like schools to keep up with our demand.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won

utterances.speaker: Julie Won

utterances.text: In a letter to my office on November 13th, SCA shared that the potential relocation site has been identified for DOT to use at 4415 45th Avenue.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: When can my office expect to receive a timeline for DOT relocation and the construction of an elementary school site?

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: And I know that Roberto knows because he's from these streets.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: You know, it's in our blood.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: So we will fight until we get every single school seat that our children are owed.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember.

chapters.summary: Won rejects the 2035 timeline, saying Long Island City builds apartments in about three years and is already behind thousands of seats. She demands a new school be cited by 2030 at 44-59 45th Avenue and vows to keep fighting with parents, PTAs, and CECs.
chapters.title: Won denounces 2035 timeline and vows to fight for school seats

summary: The Subcommittee on Landmarks, Public Sitings, Resiliency and Dispositions heard two land use items: a 537-unit 100% affordable housing project at 110 East 138th Street/63 Exterior Street in the Bronx, and two school siting applications in Long Island City, Queens.

HPD, Phipps Houses, and Douglaston Development presented the Bronx project, facing questions from Chair Marte, Council Member Encarnación, and Council Member Thomas-Henry; public witness Al Gates raised affordability, management, and environmental concerns.

SCA presented a 972-seat intermediate school and a 676-seat high school; Council Member Won pressed for timelines, elementary school seats, and transparency on the change from an elementary to middle school at the Schumann site. Both items were laid over.
title: Subcommittee on Landmarks, Public Sitings, Resiliency and Dispositions
